Late peak ischemic changes close to hour 60 can strongly signal evolving MI/low cardiac output, a direct driver of renal hypoperfusion and AKI. Max is the most pathophysiologically relevant aggregation for acute ischemic insult.
Minimum ST-change is less clinically interpretable for ischemic burden than the maximum (which captures peak deviation). Early post-op variability/artifact further limits its predictive value.
Min is generally less informative than max for detecting clinically meaningful ischemic episodes and adds collinearity. Any link to AKI is indirect via cardiac dysfunction.
Even in the leading window, minimum ST-change is not the best representation of ischemic insult compared with maximum deviation. Kept low to avoid redundancy with the more meaningful max feature.
Number of measurements reflects clinician attention/monitoring rather than a physiologic determinant of AKI. Early post-op ECG surveillance is routine, so it is weakly informative.
Measurement frequency is a behavioral proxy and not a direct AKI mechanism; ECG monitoring remains common in ICU care. Any association with severity is nonspecific.
Increased late measurement frequency may reflect concern for ongoing ischemia/hemodynamic instability, which can precede AKI, but it remains an indirect proxy. Scored low per _measured rule.

Non-specific rhythm abnormalities can correlate with hemodynamic instability and renal hypoperfusion, but the category is heterogeneous and mean aggregation blunts episodic events. In the immediate 0–12h period, many arrhythmias are transient, so conservative scoring applies.

Ventilator mode choice (ASV) is not a direct driver of AKI and is heavily influenced by institutional practice. In the immediate post-op window it mainly reflects routine ventilatory management rather than renal risk.

Minimum of a binary ventilator-mode indicator is not clinically meaningful and is redundant with max/mean. It adds little information for AKI prediction.

ASV use is an indirect marker of respiratory status and clinician preference rather than a direct AKI driver. In the 13–24h window it may correlate with overall illness severity but is not specific for renal injury.
Measurement frequency reflects documentation/monitoring behavior more than physiology. In the immediate 0–12h post-op period it is common and nonspecific for AKI risk.
Counts of ASV entries primarily reflect care processes and ventilator charting frequency. It is not a mechanistic predictor of creatinine rise.
More frequent ASV documentation late may indicate ongoing respiratory instability and higher acuity, which can track with AKI risk. Still, it is a behavioral proxy and not kidney-specific.

Controlled ventilation early post-cardiac surgery is common and often transient, making it a weak and nonspecific marker for AKI. Mean exposure also smooths short episodes of instability that would be more relevant.

Persistent controlled ventilation into 13–24h can reflect delayed recovery/greater severity, indirectly associated with AKI. As a mean aggregation, it is less informative than a clear indicator of prolonged dependence.

Any controlled mode use in 0–12h is expected after surgery and not specific for renal hypoperfusion. As an extreme indicator it captures presence, but early timing limits prognostic value (cap at 3; scored conservatively).

Frequency of controlled-mode charting is a documentation/acuity proxy rather than a physiologic determinant of AKI. In 0–12h it is routine and nonspecific.
More frequent controlled-mode entries may indicate ongoing ventilator dependence and higher acuity, indirectly linked to AKI. Still, it is a behavioral proxy and not kidney-specific.

Late frequent controlled-mode documentation can signal persistent critical illness closer to the 60h creatinine outcome, modestly increasing relevance. However it remains a monitoring/behavioral measure rather than a direct AKI mechanism.
SIMV use early is common during post-op weaning and is not a direct driver of AKI. Mean aggregation reduces sensitivity to brief episodes of instability that would matter more for renal perfusion.

SIMV in 13–24h may reflect slower liberation from ventilation and overall severity, indirectly associated with AKI. As a mean measure it is less specific than a clear indicator of prolonged ventilator dependence.

SIMV use suggests ongoing ventilatory support and illness severity, which can correlate with AKI risk via hemodynamic/PEEP effects. As a mode indicator (and using an extreme aggregation), it is an indirect proxy rather than a direct renal driver.

Measurement frequency reflects documentation/monitoring behavior rather than physiology. In 0–12h it is especially routine post-op care and not specific for impending AKI.
This is a behavioral proxy (how often mode was recorded) and not a mechanistic AKI predictor. At most it reflects general acuity, so low importance.

Spontaneous modes can indicate lighter support and potentially better hemodynamics, indirectly relating to renal perfusion. However in 0–12h this is often driven by weaning protocols and transient post-op practice (max score capped).
Presence of spontaneous ventilation may reflect recovery trajectory and lower severity, indirectly associated with lower AKI risk. Still an indirect proxy and not a direct renal insult marker.

Any time spent in spontaneous mode early may suggest faster stabilization, which can correlate with less AKI risk. In 0–12h this remains heavily influenced by routine extubation pathways, so conservative scoring.
Intermittent spontaneous mode during 13–24h can indicate improving respiratory/hemodynamic status, indirectly lowering AKI risk. Not a direct physiologic kidney marker.

Minimum spontaneous mode is a weakly interpretable binary (often just reflects continuous controlled ventilation). It is an indirect severity marker at best and not kidney-specific.
Measurement frequency is a documentation/monitoring proxy rather than physiology. In the immediate post-op period it is routine and not informative for AKI risk.
How often spontaneous mode is recorded reflects care processes more than patient physiology. Weak and non-specific for predicting creatinine rise.

Sustained MAP relates to renal perfusion, but the mean can mask hypotensive episodes that drive AKI; prefer MAP_min for pathology. In the 13–24h epoch, this is only an indirect trajectory marker.

Average MAP near the outcome window reflects overall perfusion support but can miss brief renal-insult hypotension; MAP_min is typically more predictive. Kept low to reduce collinearity with more informative extremes.
High MAP peaks early post-op are not a typical direct trigger for AKI compared with hypotension/low perfusion. In the immediate 0–12h period, transient hypertension is common and less prognostic.
MAP maxima generally reflect pressor targets or transient hypertension rather than renal hypoperfusion risk. Provides limited incremental AKI signal versus MAP_min.
Late MAP peaks are usually treatment-related and not a direct mechanism for AKI. Extremes on the high side are less relevant than hypotensive nadirs for kidney injury.

Persistent or recurrent hypotension in the trajectory phase is a strong driver of renal hypoperfusion and AKI risk. MAP_min captures the clinically relevant insult better than mean/max.

Hypotension closest to hour 60 is a leading indicator of inadequate renal perfusion and impending creatinine rise. MAP_min is a direct physiologic trigger for AKI and is highly prognostic in this late window.
Measurement frequency reflects monitoring intensity rather than physiology; arterial lines are routine after cardiac surgery. In 0–12h, high measurement counts are expected and not specific for AKI.
Arterial MAP measurement frequency is largely standard-of-care and more a proxy for ICU workflow than renal risk. Limited specificity for impending AKI.
Continued frequent MAP recording mainly indicates ongoing invasive monitoring, not a direct renal mechanism. Weak and nonspecific proxy for acuity.
NPO status early post-op is routine and not mechanistically linked to AKI beyond general illness severity. Provides minimal specific prognostic information for creatinine rise.
Remaining NPO at 13–24h may reflect slower recovery but is an indirect, nonspecific marker for AKI risk. Not a primary driver of renal injury.

Prolonged NPO by 25–36h can correlate with ongoing critical illness, delayed extubation, or hemodynamic instability, indirectly increasing AKI risk. Still nonspecific and not a direct renal biomarker.
Any NPO in the first 12h is expected after cardiac surgery and does not specifically predict AKI. Largely reflects routine perioperative care.
Being NPO at any point in 13–24h is common and nonspecific; it is not a direct determinant of renal perfusion or nephrotoxicity. Weak proxy for severity at best.
Persistent NPO status late (25–36h) can be an indirect marker of ongoing critical illness, ileus, or instability that correlates with AKI risk, but it is not a physiologic driver of renal injury.
Early post-op NPO is routine after cardiac surgery and provides little specific information about renal perfusion or tubular injury in the immediate 0–12h window.
Being at least intermittently NPO in 13–24h is common and nonspecific; it weakly reflects acuity and is not a direct AKI predictor.
The minimum NPO indicator is not informative (many patients will have some non-NPO time); it is less pathologically meaningful than sustained NPO and adds collinearity.
Measurement frequency reflects documentation/ordering behavior rather than renal physiology, and in 0–12h it is largely routine post-op charting.
How often diet/NPO is recorded is a behavioral proxy and not a mechanistic AKI predictor; at most it reflects general acuity.

Average diet status in the immediate post-op period is dominated by routine NPO/slow advancement and is not a meaningful renal risk signal.

Failure to advance diet by 25–36h can correlate with ongoing critical illness and thus AKI risk, but the mean aggregation is a diluted, indirect marker.
Achieving any diet intake early may indicate faster stabilization, but in 0–12h this is uncommon and heavily protocol-driven, limiting AKI specificity.
Reaching diet at any point in 13–24h may reflect improving trajectory and lower illness severity, but it remains an indirect proxy for AKI risk.
Having diet by 25–36h suggests clinical stability and may inversely correlate with AKI, but it is still a nonspecific surrogate rather than a renal biomarker.

The minimum diet indicator is a weak, redundant summary that does not capture a specific renal insult or established AKI mechanism.

Still primarily reflects monitoring intensity rather than renal physiology, and is heavily confounded by unit protocols. Weak predictor of creatinine trajectory.

This minimum (binary) feature is not a clear marker of severity or renal hypoperfusion and is likely redundant with other oxygen support variables. It has weak clinical specificity for predicting creatinine rise.

Measurement frequency reflects documentation/monitoring behavior rather than a physiologic mechanism for AKI. In the immediate post-op period, frequent recording is routine and not specific to renal risk.
Counts of measurements primarily capture care intensity/workflow and are not direct predictors of renal injury. Any association with AKI would be indirect and weak.

More frequent oxygen-device documentation late may reflect higher acuity or respiratory instability, which can correlate with AKI risk. Still, it is a behavioral proxy and should be down-weighted versus physiologic variables.

High-flow oxygen use suggests greater respiratory/cardiac compromise that can contribute to renal hypoxia/hypoperfusion, but early post-op support is often transient. Mean use is less informative than escalation/extremes and capped in 0–12h.

Ongoing high-flow oxygen requirement in 13–24h more strongly suggests persistent cardiopulmonary dysfunction, which is an established contributor to AKI risk via low output/hypoxemia. As a mean indicator it is still indirect and potentially collinear with max.

Sustained high-flow oxygen need close to the outcome window indicates significant ongoing illness severity that can predispose to AKI through hypoxemia and hemodynamic compromise. It remains an indirect marker rather than a renal biomarker.

Any high-flow oxygen requirement in the first 12h can mark a more severe immediate post-op course (e.g., pulmonary edema/low cardiac output), which is linked to AKI risk. However, early derangements are common and transient, so the score is conservatively capped.

High-flow oxygen at any point in 13–24h indicates significant respiratory/cardiac instability beyond the immediate post-op period, which strongly correlates with low-output states and renal hypoperfusion. As an extreme/escalation marker, it is more informative than mean use.

Need for high-flow oxygen late (25–36h) suggests ongoing respiratory failure/low cardiac output physiology and higher illness severity, which can reduce renal perfusion and increase AKI risk. It is indirect (not kidney-specific) but clinically meaningful this close to the outcome.

In the immediate 0–12h post-op period, transient oxygen support needs are common and often reflect routine post-anesthesia/CPB effects rather than evolving AKI. The minimum value is also less informative than persistent or peak support.

Ongoing need for high-flow oxygen in 13–24h can indicate slower recovery and higher severity, which may correlate with AKI risk via hypoxemia/hemodynamic stress. As a minimum/indirect marker, it is weaker than later or peak support.

Persistent requirement for high-flow oxygen in 25–36h implies sustained cardiopulmonary dysfunction and higher risk of renal hypoperfusion. Still an indirect severity marker rather than a direct renal biomarker.

Measurement frequency reflects documentation/monitoring behavior in the immediate post-op window and is not a physiologic driver of AKI. Early post-op monitoring is routine and poorly specific for impending renal injury.
How often high-flow oxygen device status is recorded mainly reflects care intensity and charting practices rather than renal pathophysiology. It is a weak, nonspecific proxy for acuity.

More frequent documentation of high-flow oxygen late may reflect clinician concern about persistent respiratory failure and overall instability, which can co-occur with AKI. Still primarily a behavioral/acuity proxy, not a direct mechanism.
First-degree AV block documentation frequency is largely a monitoring artifact and usually hemodynamically benign. In 0–12h, conduction changes are common post-op and not specific for AKI risk.
Frequency of noting first-degree AV block is not a direct predictor of renal injury and is often incidental. It provides minimal incremental information beyond overall illness severity.

Even late, first-degree AV block is typically not associated with meaningful hypotension or renal hypoperfusion, and 'measured' reflects documentation rather than physiology. Thus it has weak relevance to creatinine rise.

Higher-grade AV block can cause bradycardia/low cardiac output and renal hypoperfusion, but in 0–12h it may be transient and treated promptly (pacing/pressors). As a 'measured' feature, it is also partly documentation-driven.

Persistent or recurrent high-grade block in 13–24h can signal ongoing hemodynamic instability that increases AKI risk, but measurement frequency remains an indirect proxy. The physiologic link is plausible but not kidney-specific.

Late high-grade block can be clinically important for renal perfusion, yet this variable captures how often it is recorded rather than its severity/duration. Therefore it is only an indirect indicator of instability related to AKI.
Bundle branch block is often a baseline or perioperative conduction finding and usually not directly tied to renal perfusion. In 0–12h, documentation frequency is routine and nonspecific for AKI.
BBB documentation frequency provides little mechanistic information about renal injury and is commonly incidental. It is a weak proxy for acuity at best.

Even close to the outcome, BBB itself is not a strong driver of AKI unless associated with broader cardiogenic shock, which this 'measured' variable does not capture. Thus relevance to creatinine_ratio is minimal.

Ionized calcium reflects transfusion/citrate load and overall physiologic stress but is not a direct AKI driver; early post-bypass abnormalities are often transient. Mean is less informative than extremes for acute instability, and 0–12h is a noisy period.

Persistent calcium derangements may correlate with ongoing critical illness and vasopressor needs, indirectly affecting renal perfusion. Mean aggregation is less specific than min/max for clinically relevant hypocalcemic episodes.

Later sustained calcium abnormalities can mark ongoing severity of illness but are not established direct predictors of creatinine rise. Mean is still less pathophysiologically specific than extremes for renal hypoperfusion risk.

Hypercalcemia is uncommon early post-cardiac surgery and is not a typical trigger for AKI in this setting. In the immediate 0–12h window, isolated maxima are often treatment-related and not prognostic.

Elevated ionized calcium is not a recognized driver of postoperative AKI compared with hemodynamics, nephrotoxins, or renal labs. Max values are more likely supplementation-related than reflective of renal injury risk.
Even close to the outcome window, calcium maxima generally reflect replacement practices rather than renal pathophysiology. Not a strong or direct predictor of creatinine_ratio.

Hypocalcemia can accompany massive transfusion/citrate exposure and hemodynamic instability, which can impair renal perfusion. Still, in 0–12h it is often transient and treatment-responsive, capping importance.

Ongoing hypocalcemia may indicate persistent critical illness, transfusion burden, or shock physiology that can contribute to AKI risk. Minimum captures clinically relevant episodes better than mean/max.

Late hypocalcemic episodes can be a marker of ongoing instability and high-acuity care, indirectly increasing AKI risk via renal hypoperfusion. Min is the most relevant aggregation for potential physiologic insult among calcium summaries.
Measurement frequency mainly reflects monitoring intensity after surgery rather than a causal mechanism for AKI. Early frequent checks are routine in post-cardiac surgery ICU care.
Ordering frequency is a behavioral proxy for acuity and is not a direct physiologic predictor of creatinine rise. Calcium checks remain common in many post-op protocols.

More frequent calcium measurement later may reflect clinician concern for ongoing instability or transfusion/electrolyte issues, indirectly correlating with AKI risk. Still, it is not mechanistic and should be kept low.

Magnesium abnormalities can reflect critical illness, diuretic use, and arrhythmia management, but are not direct AKI biomarkers. Mean values in the immediate post-op window are often influenced by routine replacement.

Sustained magnesium derangements may correlate with severity of illness and medication exposure (e.g., diuretics), indirectly affecting renal risk. Mean aggregation is less informative than extremes for acute physiologic insult.

Later magnesium trends can reflect ongoing diuresis, nutrition, and replacement practices rather than renal injury itself. Mean is a nonspecific marker compared with hemodynamics and kidney-specific labs.

Early postoperative magnesium maxima are commonly due to prophylactic replacement (e.g., for arrhythmia prevention) and are not a typical cause of AKI. In 0–12h, isolated high values are rarely prognostic for creatinine_ratio.

Hypermagnesemia is usually iatrogenic (replacement/renal clearance) and is not a primary AKI driver; it may weakly reflect reduced GFR or illness severity. Max is more informative than mean, but still indirect.
Later hypermagnesemia can reflect impaired renal excretion or aggressive repletion, but it is not a direct AKI biomarker. As an extreme, it may add limited signal about declining clearance.

Early hypomagnesemia is common post-CPB and with diuresis and is not specific for AKI. The minimum may reflect electrolyte wasting/therapy rather than renal injury; capped due to indirectness and early epoch.

Hypomagnesemia can accompany diuretic use and ongoing losses and may correlate with overall instability, but it is not an established predictor of creatinine rise. Minimum is the most relevant aggregation but remains indirect.
Persistent low magnesium may indicate ongoing diuresis or poor nutritional/ICU status rather than renal dysfunction. It has at best an indirect association with AKI risk.
Measurement frequency mainly reflects routine post-op electrolyte monitoring and clinician behavior rather than renal pathophysiology. In the immediate post-op window it is especially non-specific.
Ordering frequency is a weak proxy for acuity and is commonly protocol-driven after cardiac surgery. It does not directly indicate impending AKI.
More frequent magnesium checks later may reflect ongoing electrolyte replacement/diuresis or concern for renal clearance, but it remains a behavioral proxy. At most it weakly signals higher acuity.

Average base excess early after surgery is influenced by CPB, fluids, and ventilation and is often transient. Mean smooths extremes that better capture hypoperfusion-related metabolic acidosis linked to AKI.
Sustained metabolic acidosis can reflect ongoing hypoperfusion and is associated with AKI risk, but the mean dilutes clinically important nadirs. Use of mean is therefore only indirectly informative.

Persistently abnormal base excess closer to hour 60 can indicate ongoing metabolic acidosis from shock/poor perfusion, which is a meaningful AKI risk factor. Still, mean is less specific than the minimum for capturing worst hypoperfusion.

A high (more positive) base excess generally reflects alkalosis (e.g., bicarbonate administration) and is not a typical trigger for AKI. In the immediate post-op period it is rarely prognostic for creatinine rise.
Positive base excess is usually treatment-related or reflects alkalosis and is not a direct marker of renal hypoperfusion. Max provides little AKI-specific information.
Later alkalosis/positive base excess is not a recognized driver of AKI and often reflects therapy (diuretics, bicarbonate). It is unlikely to add predictive value for creatinine_ratio.

The nadir base excess captures worst metabolic acidosis from hypoperfusion/low cardiac output, a known contributor to AKI, but early post-CPB derangements are often transient. Score capped by 0–12h epoch maximum.

A low (more negative) base excess minimum in 13–24h suggests ongoing metabolic acidosis from persistent hypoperfusion/shock, which strongly predicts subsequent AKI. The minimum best captures the pathologic insult compared with mean/max.
A very negative base excess late (25–36h) reflects significant metabolic acidosis from hypoperfusion/lactate burden, which is strongly associated with renal ischemia and subsequent AKI.
Measurement frequency mainly reflects clinician monitoring behavior in the immediate post-op period and is not a direct physiologic driver of AKI.
Ordering frequency is a weak proxy for acuity and adds little mechanistic information about renal injury risk.
More frequent checks late may indicate concern for shock/acid-base derangements that correlate with AKI risk, but it remains an indirect behavioral marker.
Test frequency early post-op is largely routine/monitoring and does not directly predict creatinine rise.
Measurement count is an indirect proxy for concern about hepatic dysfunction/hemolysis and is not a primary AKI predictor.
Late increased monitoring may reflect evolving cholestasis/low-flow state that can co-occur with AKI, but it is still indirect.
Early leukocytosis is common after surgery/CPB and is nonspecific; mean values smooth peaks and are less informative for AKI triggers.
Sustained inflammation/infection can contribute to AKI risk, but mean WBC is nonspecific and less predictive than extremes.
Persistent leukocytosis closer to the outcome may indicate infection/SIRS driving renal hypoperfusion and nephrotoxic exposure, giving moderate predictive value.
A high WBC peak can signal early SIRS/occult infection, but in the immediate post-op window it is often transient and nonspecific (capped by epoch rule).
A WBC spike during the trajectory phase may reflect evolving infection/inflammation associated with AKI, though it remains indirect.
A marked WBC peak late (25–36h) suggests significant infection/SIRS, which is strongly linked to AKI via cytokine-mediated injury and hemodynamic instability.
Low WBC early is uncommon and often reflects dilution/lab variability; it has weak and nonspecific linkage to AKI risk.
WBC nadir is generally less informative than peaks for AKI risk and may reflect non-pathologic factors (hemodilution, sampling).
A late low WBC could indicate severe illness/immunosuppression or marrow suppression, but its relationship to AKI is indirect and weaker than WBC maxima.
Measurement frequency mainly reflects clinician concern/inflammation workup rather than a direct AKI mechanism, and early post-op labs are routine. Per rules, _measured features are weak proxies.
Ordering frequency is a behavioral/acuity marker and not a physiologic driver of AKI. In this mid window it remains largely routine post-cardiac surgery monitoring.
More frequent WBC checks late may reflect evolving infection/sepsis concern, which can precipitate AKI, but it is still an indirect behavioral proxy. Therefore capped low per _measured rule.

Coagulopathy can correlate with hepatic dysfunction/bleeding/transfusion and overall severity, indirectly increasing AKI risk, but mean PT blunts acute extremes. In the immediate post-op period, transient PT elevation is common, so conservative scoring applies.

Persistently prolonged PT may indicate ongoing coagulopathy/critical illness and correlate with complications that raise AKI risk, but the mean is less informative than extremes for acute insults. Capped to reduce collinearity with max/min PT.

A high PT/INR extreme can signal significant coagulopathy (bleeding risk, transfusion, shock) associated with renal hypoperfusion and AKI. However, early post-bypass anticoagulation effects are common, so max score limited in 0–12h.

Late extreme PT prolongation suggests clinically significant ongoing coagulopathy/organ dysfunction and higher likelihood of bleeding/transfusion or shock states that contribute to AKI. Max captures the pathologic insult better than mean, so it is prioritized.
A low/normal PT minimum is not a plausible trigger for AKI and mainly reflects periods without coagulopathy. As an extreme, the minimum is not the pathologic direction for renal risk here.
The minimum PT value does not represent a renal insult and is unlikely to predict creatinine rise compared with prolonged PT extremes. It adds redundancy without capturing pathology.
PT measurement frequency is largely protocolized after cardiac surgery and reflects monitoring rather than a causal AKI pathway. Per rules, _measured features should be scored 1–2.
Ordering frequency is a weak proxy for acuity/bleeding concern and not a direct physiologic predictor of AKI. Continued PT checks are common in post-op management.

More frequent PT checks late may indicate active bleeding/anticoagulation management or hepatic dysfunction, which can accompany hemodynamic instability and AKI risk. Still a behavioral proxy, so kept low.

NRBCs can reflect hypoxemia, inflammation, or severe physiologic stress that correlates with AKI risk, but the mean dilutes acute spikes. Early post-op stress responses are common, so conservative scoring.
Ongoing NRBC presence suggests sustained critical illness/hypoxia which is associated with AKI, but mean aggregation is less specific than extremes. Mid-epoch scoring is moderated per temporal rule.

Persistently elevated NRBCs late can mark ongoing hypoperfusion/hypoxemia and severity of illness linked to AKI, but mean is still an indirect marker. Capped to avoid redundancy with max NRBC features.

An early NRBC spike can indicate significant hypoxia/physiologic stress and correlates with worse outcomes including AKI, and max captures this better than mean. However, immediate post-op derangements are common, so capped at 3 in 0–12h.

Elevated NRBCs can reflect severe physiologic stress, hypoxemia, or inflammation, which may correlate with multiorgan dysfunction including AKI, but it is not kidney-specific. Max is the most relevant aggregation, yet in this mid-epoch it remains an indirect marker.

Persistently high NRBCs closer to the outcome can indicate ongoing hypoxia/critical illness and has been associated with worse ICU outcomes, which can track with AKI risk. Still indirect and not a renal biomarker.
The minimum NRBC value is not pathologic and does not capture the stress signal that would relate to AKI risk. Early post-op values are also commonly transient and nonspecific.
NRBC minimum provides little clinical information about severity of illness or hypoxic stress relevant to AKI. It is largely redundant/non-informative compared with maxima.
A low/minimum NRBC does not indicate a mechanism for AKI and is not a recognized predictor. The max would be the clinically meaningful direction if any.
Measurement frequency mainly reflects ordering behavior and routine CBC differentials rather than renal physiology. In the immediate post-op window it is especially nonspecific for impending AKI.
How often NRBCs are measured is a weak proxy for acuity and is not a direct driver of AKI. Typically reflects lab panel frequency rather than kidney-focused concern.

More frequent measurement late may reflect clinician concern for ongoing critical illness/hemolysis/hypoxia, which can co-occur with AKI risk. Still primarily a behavioral proxy, not a physiologic mechanism.

Stress hyperglycemia is associated with worse outcomes and may correlate with AKI risk, but mean values dilute short hyperglycemic spikes. In the immediate post-op period glucose is heavily protocol-driven (insulin infusions), limiting specificity.

Sustained dysglycemia can reflect severity of illness and is linked to AKI risk, but mean glucose remains an indirect marker and may be influenced by insulin protocols. Not as informative as extremes for acute insult.

Persistently elevated mean glucose closer to hour 60 can indicate ongoing stress/infection/catecholamine exposure and is associated with higher AKI risk. Still indirect and less specific than hemodynamics or renal labs.

Acute hyperglycemic peaks can signal severe stress response and are associated with postoperative complications including AKI, making max more informative than mean/min. Score capped by early epoch where transient derangements are common.

Higher glucose maxima during the trajectory phase can indicate ongoing stress, infection, or high catecholamine dose, all associated with AKI risk. Max captures the insult better than mean, but remains indirect.

Late hyperglycemic spikes can be a strong marker of persistent critical illness (sepsis, high-dose vasopressors/steroids) and correlate with AKI development. Max best captures the pathologic excursion compared with mean/min.

Hypoglycemia can reflect overtreatment with insulin or hepatic dysfunction and is associated with adverse outcomes, but it is not a primary AKI mechanism. Early post-op lows are often iatrogenic and transient.

Low glucose may indicate insulin overcorrection or severe illness and can correlate with worse outcomes, but links to AKI are indirect. Minimum is less informative than maxima for stress-related AKI risk.

Hypoglycemia can reflect critical illness severity and is associated with worse outcomes, but it is not a primary mechanistic driver of post-cardiac surgery AKI compared with hemodynamics and renal labs. As an extreme it may capture stress/insulin effects, but remains an indirect predictor.

Measurement frequency mainly reflects ICU monitoring intensity and insulin protocol use rather than renal physiology. In the immediate 0–12h post-op period, frequent glucose checks are routine and weakly informative for AKI.
Glucose check frequency is a behavioral/acuity proxy and not a direct renal perfusion or nephrotoxin marker. In 13–24h it remains largely protocol-driven and weak for predicting creatinine rise.

Later frequent glucose monitoring may indicate ongoing instability (vasopressors, nutrition changes, insulin infusion) and higher illness severity, which can correlate with AKI risk. Still, it is not a physiologic kidney injury marker, so importance is limited.

Lower platelets can reflect CPB-related consumption/hemodilution and systemic inflammation, which are associated with AKI risk, but early post-op values are often transient. Mean is less informative than nadir for capturing clinically relevant thrombocytopenia.

Persistent thrombocytopenia may track ongoing inflammation/bleeding/transfusion and overall severity, indirectly relating to AKI. However, the mean blunts the prognostic signal compared with the minimum platelet count.

In the 25–36h window, sustained thrombocytopenia can indicate ongoing critical illness and microvascular dysfunction, which may accompany AKI. Still, mean is collinear with and less pathophysiologically specific than the platelet minimum.

A high platelet maximum is rarely a trigger for AKI and is often clinically uninformative in the immediate post-CPB period. Extremes on the high side do not capture the relevant pathology for renal injury.
Platelet maxima generally do not reflect a mechanism leading to AKI; thrombocytopenia is the more relevant signal. This aggregation is likely redundant and weakly predictive.

Higher platelet peaks are not a recognized driver of post-operative AKI and add little beyond other severity markers. The clinically meaningful platelet signal for AKI risk is the nadir rather than the maximum.

Early platelet nadir can reflect CPB-related consumption, bleeding, and inflammatory activation, which correlate with subsequent organ dysfunction including AKI. In 0–12h many drops are transient, so the score is capped and conservative.

A low platelet nadir in 13–24h suggests persistent consumption/bleeding/sepsis-like physiology and higher illness severity, which is associated with AKI. The minimum captures the relevant insult better than mean/max.

A low platelet nadir close to the outcome window can indicate ongoing systemic inflammation, microvascular dysfunction, or complications (bleeding/transfusion/sepsis) that strongly track with AKI risk. As an extreme in the leading-indicator epoch, it is a stronger predictor than mean/max.

Platelet measurement frequency is largely routine post-cardiac surgery lab surveillance and reflects practice patterns more than kidney injury biology. In 0–12h it is especially protocolized and weak for AKI prediction.
Ordering frequency is a behavioral proxy for acuity and is not a direct renal injury marker. It may reflect bleeding concern but remains weak and non-specific for predicting creatinine ratio.

More frequent platelet checks later may indicate ongoing bleeding, transfusion needs, or clinical deterioration, which can co-occur with AKI. Nonetheless it is an indirect, practice-driven signal and should remain low importance.

Mean corpuscular hemoglobin (MCH) is not a direct marker of renal perfusion or tubular injury; perioperative shifts are usually unrelated to AKI biology. As a 0–12h mean, it is also unlikely to capture a specific renal insult.
MCH has minimal physiologic linkage to postoperative AKI risk compared with hemodynamics, nephrotoxins, and renal labs. The mean value in this epoch is unlikely to add prognostic signal.
Even close to the outcome window, MCH is not an established predictor of AKI and mainly reflects erythrocyte indices rather than kidney injury. Any association would be indirect and weak.

An elevated MCH maximum does not represent a known acute trigger for AKI after cardiac surgery. In the immediate postoperative period, this is more likely noise/measurement variability than renal-relevant pathology.
MCH maxima are not clinically used to assess renal hypoperfusion or nephrotoxic injury. This extreme is unlikely to provide meaningful AKI prediction signal.
A late-epoch MCH maximum still lacks a plausible direct mechanism linking it to creatinine rise. It is not a recognized biomarker or driver of postoperative AKI.

MCH minimum is not an established AKI risk factor and does not directly reflect renal perfusion or injury. Any relationship would be highly indirect.
Even as a leading indicator window, MCH minimum is not clinically informative for AKI prediction compared with creatinine, urine output, lactate, MAP, or vasopressor needs. Likely redundant/noise.
Measurement frequency mainly reflects routine CBC ordering after surgery rather than specific concern for AKI. As a behavioral proxy, it provides weak and nonspecific signal.
CBC/MCH measurement counts are largely driven by standard ICU protocols and anemia/bleeding surveillance, not renal-specific suspicion. Thus it is a weak proxy for AKI risk.
Even later, MCH measurement frequency is more related to hematology monitoring than kidney injury evaluation. As a _measured feature, it should remain low importance.

Dysnatremias can reflect fluid balance, neurohormonal stress, and severity of illness, which are indirectly related to AKI risk. However, in the immediate 0–12h period sodium shifts are often iatrogenic/transient, so predictive value is limited.

Sustained sodium abnormalities may indicate ongoing fluid/diuretic management issues and illness severity that correlate with AKI risk. Still, sodium is not a direct renal injury biomarker, so importance remains modest.

Persistent dysnatremia closer to hour 60 can reflect ongoing volume derangements, diuretic response, and neurohormonal activation that track with evolving renal dysfunction. As a mean (not an extreme), it is less specific than max/min but can still carry moderate prognostic signal.

Hypernatremia extremes can indicate free-water deficit or aggressive diuresis and are associated with worse outcomes, indirectly including AKI. In 0–12h, however, sodium extremes are often perioperative/iatrogenic, so the score is capped conservatively.

Hypernatremia can reflect free-water deficit/diuresis and overall illness severity, which may correlate with AKI risk, but it is not a direct renal injury marker. As an extreme value it is more informative than a mean, yet in this mid epoch it remains an indirect predictor.

Late hypernatremia may indicate ongoing dehydration, osmotic diuresis, or aggressive diuresis, which can worsen renal perfusion. Still, sodium is a nonspecific electrolyte signal rather than a direct AKI biomarker.

Early postoperative hyponatremia is common from hemodilution/fluids and stress physiology and is usually transient. It is an indirect marker of fluid balance rather than a primary driver of AKI, and the 0–12h window is de-emphasized.

Hyponatremia in this phase can reflect fluid overload, low effective arterial volume, or SIADH-like physiology, which may accompany AKI-prone states. However it remains nonspecific and not a direct predictor of creatinine rise.

Persistent or late hyponatremia may track with fluid overload/low effective circulating volume and higher acuity, which can be associated with AKI. Sodium itself is not mechanistically specific for tubular injury, so importance is limited.

Measurement frequency mainly reflects routine ICU lab monitoring immediately after cardiac surgery rather than specific AKI physiology. In the initial 0–12h period it is especially driven by protocolized care.
How often sodium is checked is largely a behavioral/protocol signal and only weakly reflects concern for dysnatremia or volume issues. It is not a direct indicator of impending creatinine rise.

More frequent sodium checks later may indicate ongoing instability in fluids/diuresis or clinician concern, which can correlate with AKI risk. Still, it is a behavioral proxy and should remain low importance.

Ordering TEG platelet aggregation is primarily related to bleeding/coagulopathy management after surgery, not kidney injury mechanisms. In the immediate postoperative window it is common and not specific for AKI prediction.

Late TEG platelet aggregation testing suggests ongoing bleeding/coagulopathy evaluation, which is not a direct driver of creatinine rise. It is a behavioral marker with weak and nonspecific linkage to AKI.

MCHC has no established relationship to postoperative AKI beyond very nonspecific illness effects. It is unlikely to add predictive value for creatinine_ratio.
Even close to the outcome window, MCHC remains a nonspecific hematologic index without a plausible direct pathway to AKI. Any correlation would be incidental rather than causal or predictive.
An extreme MCHC value is more likely due to lab artifact, transfusion effects, or hemoconcentration than a kidney-specific process. In the 0–12h epoch it provides no meaningful AKI signal.

MCHC extremes can reflect hemoconcentration or lab artifact/hemolysis but are not a primary AKI driver. Compared with hemodynamics/creatinine/urine output, it is an indirect and nonspecific signal.
Early postoperative MCHC lows are common from hemodilution/transfusion and are not directly linked to renal tubular injury. In the 0–12h epoch, transient shifts are expected and weakly predictive.
Low MCHC in this window is still a nonspecific anemia/hemodilution marker and not an established AKI predictor. Any association is indirect via overall illness severity.
Persistently low MCHC may correlate with ongoing bleeding/hemodilution and higher acuity, which can secondarily affect renal perfusion. It remains nonspecific and not a direct kidney injury marker.
Measurement frequency reflects ordering behavior (CBC monitoring) rather than physiology. In immediate post-op care this is routine and not specific for impending AKI.
CBC/MCHC rechecks in this period usually reflect routine monitoring or anemia/bleeding evaluation, not kidney-specific concern. As a behavioral proxy it has weak AKI specificity.
More frequent MCHC checks may indicate ongoing instability but is not a kidney-directed test and is highly practice-pattern dependent. Therefore it provides minimal independent AKI signal.

High hematocrit early post-op often reflects hemoconcentration or transfusion and is not a typical direct trigger for AKI in this setting. In 0–12h it is especially confounded by fluid shifts.
A high maximum hematocrit is generally less relevant than low nadirs for renal hypoxia risk. Any link to AKI via hemoconcentration is indirect and inconsistent.

Later hemoconcentration could indicate dehydration/over-diuresis and reduced renal perfusion, but this is still an indirect and nonspecific mechanism. The maximum is less informative than hypotensive episodes or low hematocrit nadirs.

A low hematocrit nadir can reflect significant anemia/hemodilution and reduced oxygen delivery, which is a recognized contributor to postoperative AKI risk. Score capped by the 0–12h epoch where transient nadirs are common.

A low nadir in this window suggests ongoing anemia/bleeding or inadequate recovery, which can impair renal oxygen delivery and correlate with severity of illness. Minimum is more pathophysiologically relevant than mean/max for AKI risk.

A low hematocrit nadir close to hour 60 strongly suggests persistent anemia/bleeding/hemodilution and reduced renal oxygen delivery, which is linked to postoperative AKI. As an extreme value in the leading-indicator window, it is more predictive than mean/max.
Measurement frequency mainly reflects routine post-op CBC monitoring rather than a renal mechanism. In the immediate 0–12h period it is especially nonspecific for later creatinine rise.
CBC ordering frequency is a weak behavioral proxy for acuity and not a direct AKI driver. By 13–24h it still adds little specific signal for creatinine_ratio.
Later CBC measurement frequency may reflect ongoing instability/bleeding workup but is not physiologic evidence of AKI. As a utilization feature it should remain low importance.
Basophil count has no established relationship to renal hypoperfusion or tubular injury after cardiac surgery. The mean in the immediate post-op window is unlikely to predict creatinine_ratio.
Basophil mean is not a recognized AKI risk factor or biomarker in this context. Any association would be indirect and likely noise.

Basophil maxima do not capture a kidney perfusion insult or nephrotoxic exposure. Not clinically informative for predicting creatinine_ratio.

Frequency of differential counts is largely routine with CBCs and reflects ordering behavior, not renal physiology. In the early post-op period it is not specific for impending AKI.

Even close to the outcome window, ordering frequency of basophils is nonspecific and not mechanistically tied to AKI. Should remain minimal importance.

Persistent lymphopenia may indicate ongoing systemic inflammation/sepsis risk that can contribute to AKI indirectly. Still nonspecific and not a primary AKI predictor.

Trough measurement suggests ongoing vancomycin with potential nephrotoxic risk and concern for accumulation, indirectly related to AKI. Not a direct physiologic predictor.
Later trough monitoring may reflect reduced renal clearance and higher nephrotoxicity risk, which can precede creatinine rise. Still an ordering proxy, so limited to 1–2.

Sustained hypoxemia can worsen renal medullary oxygenation and contribute to AKI, but mean SpO2 in the immediate postoperative window is often transiently affected by ventilation/anesthesia. Extremes would be more informative than mean for acute insult.

Ongoing lower average oxygenation in the trajectory phase can reflect respiratory failure/low cardiac output physiology that threatens renal oxygen delivery. Mean is less sensitive than minima, but persistent hypoxemia can be clinically meaningful.

In the closest window to outcome, sustained lower SpO2 can indicate ongoing cardiopulmonary compromise and reduced renal oxygen delivery, increasing AKI risk. Mean remains less specific than hypoxemic minima but can capture persistent dysfunction.
Maximum SpO2 largely reflects supplemental oxygen/ventilator settings and is not a marker of hypoxic insult. In 0–12h it provides little information about renal risk.
High maximum SpO2 is typically driven by oxygen therapy and does not indicate renal-threatening physiology. It is not informative for AKI compared with hypoxemia measures.
Maximum SpO2 is usually near-normal with supplemental oxygen and is not a specific driver of AKI. The minimum (hypoxemia) is the more pathologic signal, so cap to avoid collinearity.

Early postoperative hypoxemia can reflect low cardiac output, pulmonary dysfunction, or shock physiology that can reduce renal oxygen delivery. In the immediate 0–12h period derangements are often transient, so importance is capped.

Persistent or recurrent hypoxemia in the trajectory phase suggests ongoing cardiopulmonary instability and impaired systemic oxygen delivery, which increases AKI risk. Still indirect and non-specific compared with direct renal markers.

Late-window hypoxemia is a stronger leading indicator of sustained illness severity (e.g., low output, sepsis, respiratory failure) that can precipitate renal ischemia and AKI. The minimum captures the acute insult better than mean/max.
Measurement frequency mainly reflects monitoring intensity and routine ICU practice rather than a physiologic mechanism for AKI. In the immediate post-op period it is especially non-specific.
How often SpO2 is recorded is largely protocol-driven and a weak proxy for acuity. It does not directly inform renal perfusion or tubular injury.
More frequent SpO2 documentation may weakly proxy clinical concern for instability in the later window, which can correlate with AKI risk. Still behavioral/monitoring-driven rather than causal.

ALT reflects hepatocellular injury rather than renal function; mean values in the first 12h are often influenced by perioperative factors and are non-specific for AKI. Extremes would better capture shock liver if present, so mean is de-emphasized.
An early ALT spike can indicate hypoperfusion/ischemic hepatitis from low cardiac output, which can co-occur with renal ischemia. In 0–12h this is often transient and indirect, so capped.
Low/normal ALT has no meaningful physiologic link to AKI risk. It is not a marker of renal perfusion or injury.
Ordering frequency of ALT is a weak behavioral proxy (concern for liver injury) and not a direct AKI mechanism. In early post-op care it is often routine or protocolized.
ALT measurement frequency mainly reflects clinician behavior and is not specific for renal injury. It provides limited incremental signal for AKI beyond hemodynamics and renal labs.
Late repeated ALT checks may indicate ongoing shock/organ dysfunction evaluation, which can correlate with AKI risk. Still an indirect, non-renal behavioral marker so kept low.

BUN is a kidney-related marker influenced by renal perfusion, catabolism, and volume status; early elevations can suggest prerenal azotemia. In 0–12h it is less specific due to perioperative fluid shifts, so capped.

Sustained BUN elevation in the trajectory phase can reflect ongoing reduced renal perfusion or evolving renal dysfunction. It remains less specific than creatinine/urine output but is an established risk indicator.

In the 25–36h leading window, higher mean BUN more strongly suggests persistent azotemia from reduced GFR or prerenal physiology preceding creatinine rise. As a renal-related lab close to the outcome, it is a strong predictor (though not as definitive as creatinine itself).

Elevated BUN can reflect reduced renal clearance or hypoperfusion, but in the immediate post-op window it is often confounded by hemodilution, catabolism, and transfusion. As an early signal it is relevant but capped by the 0–12h epoch limit.

Persistently high or rising BUN in the trajectory phase can indicate evolving renal dysfunction or ongoing hypoperfusion. Still indirect relative to creatinine and influenced by protein load/bleeding.

High BUN closer to the outcome window more strongly suggests impaired renal clearance and/or sustained low effective circulating volume. It can be a strong predictor of subsequent creatinine rise, though not as specific as creatinine itself.
Low BUN is generally not a trigger or marker of AKI and is often driven by dilutional effects early after bypass and resuscitation. The minimum value adds little pathophysiologic signal for AKI risk.
A low minimum BUN in this window is not clinically informative for AKI prediction and is more reflective of fluid balance/nutrition than renal injury. Limited mechanistic link to creatinine rise.
Minimum BUN remains a weak and nonspecific indicator for AKI; extremes of low BUN do not capture renal insult. Adds redundancy without clear prognostic value.
Measurement frequency mainly reflects routine post-cardiac surgery lab protocols and clinician behavior rather than renal physiology. In the immediate post-op period it is especially nonspecific.
More frequent BUN checks may reflect concern for renal dysfunction or hemodynamic instability, but it is still a behavioral proxy and not a direct mechanism. Weak-to-plausible association only.
Increased ordering closer to hour 60 can indicate clinician suspicion of AKI or worsening status, but remains indirect and practice-pattern dependent. Should be kept low per the _measured rule.

Amylase testing is not directly related to AKI risk and usually reflects evaluation for pancreatitis or other abdominal pathology. In 0–12h it is unlikely to add renal-specific prognostic information.
Ordering amylase is generally unrelated to kidney perfusion or nephrotoxicity and is a weak behavioral marker at best. Minimal expected contribution to creatinine_ratio prediction.
Even near the outcome window, amylase measurement primarily signals non-renal diagnostic workup and has no established link to post-cardiac surgery AKI. Treat as low-importance behavioral noise.

Acidemia can accompany shock/low cardiac output and is associated with AKI risk, but the mean pH in the immediate post-op period is often transient and buffered by ventilation and bicarbonate. Mean aggregation also smooths the clinically relevant extremes.

Sustained lower average pH in the trajectory phase suggests ongoing hypoperfusion, sepsis, or respiratory failure, all of which increase AKI risk. Still less informative than pH minima or lactate, but clinically meaningful.

Persistently abnormal mean pH close to hour 60 indicates ongoing systemic derangement (shock/poor perfusion) that strongly predisposes to AKI. As a sustained marker of physiologic stress, it can be a strong predictor of creatinine rise.

High (alkalemic) pH is not a typical driver of AKI and often reflects ventilator settings or bicarbonate administration rather than renal injury. The maximum value is unlikely to capture the relevant insult compared with low pH extremes.
Alkalemia is usually not a primary driver of AKI; it may reflect ventilation/diuresis rather than renal injury. Also less informative than acidemia extremes for renal hypoperfusion risk.
Higher pH late can reflect overventilation or contraction alkalosis and is not a direct AKI mechanism. Acidemia (low pH) is typically the more pathologic extreme for kidney risk.

Early postoperative acidemia can indicate hypoperfusion/lactate burden during/after bypass, which is linked to AKI risk. However, in the immediate 0–12h period derangements are common/transient, capping importance.

Persistent or recurrent acidemia in the trajectory phase suggests ongoing shock/poor perfusion or severe respiratory failure, which strongly predisposes to AKI. The minimum pH captures the acute insult better than mean/max.

Late acidemia close to the outcome window is a strong marker of ongoing hypoperfusion/critical illness and correlates with subsequent creatinine rise. The minimum value best captures the harmful extreme relevant to AKI.

Measurement frequency mainly reflects clinician concern/acuity (e.g., instability, ventilation changes) rather than a direct renal mechanism. In the immediate postoperative period frequent ABGs are routine, limiting specificity for AKI.
More frequent pH checks suggest ongoing instability or ventilatory/hemodynamic management, indirectly associated with AKI risk. Still a behavioral proxy and not a physiologic driver.
Late frequent ABG/pH monitoring implies persistent critical illness, which can correlate with AKI, but it remains a non-mechanistic proxy. Therefore kept low per the _measured rule.
Cholesterol testing is not part of AKI evaluation and has no acute physiologic link to postoperative creatinine rise. Ordering in the first 12h is typically unrelated to renal trajectory.
Cholesterol measurement is generally unrelated to AKI risk stratification in the ICU and does not reflect renal perfusion or nephrotoxicity. As a behavioral proxy, it provides minimal signal.
Late cholesterol testing is not a recognized indicator of impending AKI and is unlikely to be ordered for renal concerns. Provides negligible prognostic value for creatinine_ratio.
Mean lymphocyte count early after surgery is nonspecific and heavily influenced by stress response and hemodilution. It is not an established driver or direct marker of AKI.

Sustained lymphopenia can reflect systemic inflammation/sepsis risk, which can be associated with AKI, but the mean is a weak and indirect signal. Not as informative as hemodynamics, renal labs, or nephrotoxins.
A high lymphocyte maximum in the immediate postoperative window is not mechanistically linked to AKI and is likely noise from lab variability. Extremes here do not represent a known renal insult.
Lymphocyte maxima are not clinically used to predict AKI and do not capture a renal-perfusion or nephrotoxic pathway. Provides minimal incremental value versus other inflammatory markers.
Early lymphopenia may indicate stress/inflammation and higher illness severity, indirectly associated with AKI risk. In 0–12h this is common post-bypass and nonspecific, limiting importance.

Lymphopenia can reflect stress/inflammation and overall illness severity, which indirectly correlates with AKI risk. It is not a direct renal perfusion or kidney injury marker, and using the minimum adds limited specificity.

Measurement frequency mainly reflects ordering behavior/acuity rather than a physiologic driver of AKI. Early (0–12h) labs are commonly routine post-op and are weakly informative for later creatinine rise.
This is a behavioral proxy for clinician concern rather than a mechanism of kidney injury. In the 13–24h window it may reflect general instability but is not specific for impending AKI.
More frequent CBC monitoring closer to hour 60 can indicate higher acuity or complications that co-occur with AKI risk. Still, it is indirect and non-specific, so it should remain low importance.
Glucose checks are routine in post-cardiac surgery ICU care and measurement presence is not a physiologic AKI marker. As a _measured feature in the immediate post-op period, it is weakly predictive.
Frequency/presence of glucose measurement reflects care intensity (e.g., insulin protocols) more than kidney injury biology. It has minimal specific linkage to subsequent creatinine ratio.

Increased glucose monitoring later may indicate persistent critical illness or difficult glycemic control, which can correlate with AKI risk. However it remains an indirect behavioral proxy, not a direct renal predictor.

Ordering CK early is often driven by concern for myocardial/skeletal muscle injury and is not specific for renal hypoperfusion or tubular injury. As a measurement-frequency feature in 0–12h, it is weakly informative.
CK measurement may reflect concern for rhabdomyolysis/ischemia, which can contribute to AKI, but the feature captures ordering rather than CK level. Thus it is only an indirect signal of risk.

Later CK monitoring can indicate ongoing muscle injury/low-flow states that may predispose to AKI, but this is still a proxy for clinician suspicion. Without the CK value, specificity for creatinine rise is limited.

eGFR is derived from creatinine and can reflect early renal dysfunction, but in the immediate post-op period values are often transiently affected by hemodilution and non-steady-state creatinine. Mean further smooths acute drops, so it is capped low to avoid redundancy.

Persistently reduced eGFR in the trajectory phase suggests evolving renal dysfunction and is more informative than the immediate post-op window. However, mean aggregation can dilute clinically important nadirs compared with minima.

Lower eGFR close to hour 60 is a strong direct indicator of worsening renal function and is tightly linked to subsequent creatinine ratio. Although mean smooths extremes, sustained reduction in this late window is highly predictive.

A higher (max) eGFR is not a pathologic trigger for AKI and often reflects dilutional/measurement variability early after bypass. As an extreme in the non-pathologic direction, it provides little prognostic value.
Maximum eGFR does not capture renal insult; it mainly reflects best observed value and variability. It is unlikely to predict later creatinine rise compared with low eGFR measures.

Even in the leading-indicator window, the maximum eGFR represents the least impaired moment and is not mechanistically linked to AKI progression. It is largely redundant/noisy relative to low eGFR summaries.
Low eGFR reflects reduced renal filtration and is closely tied to creatinine rise, but early post-op values can be transient/hemodilutional; capped by 0–12h max score rule.
Persistently low eGFR in the trajectory phase suggests evolving AKI rather than immediate post-bypass noise and is a strong predictor of later creatinine increase.
Low eGFR closest to hour-60 is essentially an early biomarker of impaired filtration and strongly predicts a higher creatinine_ratio.
More frequent eGFR/chemistry checks reflect clinician concern/acuity rather than a direct mechanism; early post-op monitoring is also routine.
Increased measurement frequency may indicate concern for renal dysfunction or instability, but remains a behavioral proxy rather than physiology.
Late frequent monitoring can signal suspected AKI, yet it is still indirect and should not be weighted like physiologic derangement.
LDH ordering frequency is a nonspecific behavioral marker (hemolysis/ischemia workup) and is not directly linked to AKI prediction in this context.
LDH measurement frequency remains nonspecific and more reflective of workup intensity than renal injury risk.
Even late, LDH checks are not a direct renal biomarker; frequency mainly reflects clinician suspicion for other processes (hemolysis/ischemia).
Coagulopathy can correlate with severity of illness/hepatic dysfunction and bleeding/transfusion risk, but mean INR in the immediate post-op window is often transient and indirect for AKI.
Average INR is less informative than extremes for acute bleeding/shock risk; kept low to avoid collinearity with INR_max which better captures pathologic insult.
A high INR peak may indicate significant coagulopathy/bleeding risk and overall physiologic stress that can contribute to renal hypoperfusion; capped by 0–12h max score rule.
Late INR spikes can reflect ongoing coagulopathy, bleeding/transfusion needs, or hepatic dysfunction associated with AKI risk, though still indirect compared with renal labs/hemodynamics.
Low INR is generally not a driver of AKI and is less clinically meaningful for renal outcomes than elevated INR extremes.
Low INR late is not a recognized predictor of AKI and adds little beyond other severity markers.
INR measurement frequency is largely routine post-cardiac surgery monitoring and reflects practice patterns more than renal pathophysiology.

Frequency of INR checks reflects bleeding/anticoagulation management and overall acuity rather than a direct renal mechanism. It may correlate indirectly with shock/transfusion burden that can contribute to AKI.
Later INR monitoring can indicate ongoing coagulopathy/bleeding risk and higher illness severity, which may track with AKI risk. Still a behavioral proxy, not a physiologic kidney marker.
Eosinophil percentage is not a typical driver or early marker of post-cardiac surgery AKI. The mean in the immediate post-op window is unlikely to add prognostic value.
Sustained eosinophil percentage is generally unrelated to hemodynamic/ischemic AKI after cardiac surgery. Mean aggregation further dilutes any rare signal (e.g., drug reaction).
A transient eosinophil spike could weakly suggest allergic/drug-related processes, but this is uncommon and nonspecific in early post-op care. In 0–12h, changes are often noise; capped by epoch.

An elevated maximum eosinophil percentage could indirectly flag drug hypersensitivity/interstitial nephritis risk, but this is rare and not a primary post-cardiac surgery AKI pathway. Max is the most relevant aggregation among eosinophil summaries.
Low eosinophil percentage has no meaningful mechanistic link to AKI and is often influenced by stress steroids/catecholamines. Minimum values are not clinically informative for renal risk here.
Minimum eosinophil percentage is not a recognized predictor of AKI and mainly reflects stress response variability. Provides little renal-specific information.
Measurement count largely reflects routine CBC ordering in the immediate post-op period rather than targeted AKI concern. As a behavioral proxy, it has weak specificity for renal outcomes.
CBC differential frequency is typically protocolized and not specific to impending AKI. Measurement count is a weak acuity proxy at best.

Even in the later window, eosinophil measurement frequency is usually driven by routine labs or general instability, not kidney-specific monitoring. Behavioral proxy with low specificity for creatinine rise.

Ordering LDL cholesterol post-op is not physiologically linked to acute creatinine rise and is often unrelated to ICU AKI management. As a measured/binary ordering feature, it is a weak proxy at most.
LDL testing does not reflect renal perfusion, nephrotoxicity, or early kidney injury in the ICU setting. Ordering behavior here is unlikely to track AKI risk.
LDL measurement near 36h is still not a kidney-relevant test and is unlikely to be ordered due to AKI concern. Minimal expected predictive value for creatinine_ratio.
MCV reflects chronic anemia/nutritional status rather than acute renal perfusion or tubular injury. Mean MCV in the immediate post-op period is unlikely to predict AKI; capped by epoch.
MCV is not an established predictor of post-cardiac surgery AKI and changes slowly relative to the AKI time course. Mean aggregation offers little additional signal for creatinine_ratio.
MCV is not a direct marker of renal perfusion or tubular injury; changes mainly reflect anemia/nutrition/transfusion effects. The mean value is also nonspecific for AKI prediction.
Early postoperative MCV extremes are usually driven by transfusion/fluids and are not mechanistically linked to AKI. In the 0–12h epoch, transient shifts are common and poorly predictive.
MCV maximum in this window is a nonspecific hematologic signal and not an established AKI predictor. Any association would be indirect via transfusion/bleeding rather than kidney injury.
Even close to the outcome, MCV maxima do not reflect renal function or perfusion status. It is unlikely to add independent predictive value for creatinine rise.
Low MCV reflects chronic microcytosis/iron deficiency rather than acute renal insult. In the immediate post-op period, dilutional effects further reduce specificity for AKI.
MCV minimum remains a weak, indirect proxy at best (anemia/bleeding/transfusion patterns) and is not a recognized driver of AKI. Limited physiologic linkage to creatinine trajectory.
Low MCV at 25–36h is still not a renal biomarker and does not capture hemodynamic kidney stress. Any relationship would be confounded and weak.
Measurement frequency reflects ordering behavior (CBC cadence) rather than kidney physiology. In 0–12h, CBCs are routine after cardiac surgery and not specific for AKI concern.
CBC/MCV measurement count is largely protocol-driven and a weak proxy for acuity. It does not specifically indicate impending AKI compared with renal labs or urine output monitoring.

Even in the leading-indicator window, MCV measurement frequency is nonspecific and more reflective of general instability/bleeding surveillance than renal injury. Should not be weighted highly for creatinine_ratio.

Mean platelet volume can reflect inflammation/platelet activation, which may correlate with postoperative complications, but it is not a direct AKI marker. In 0–12h, values are often perturbed by CPB and transfusion, limiting specificity.
Sustained MPV elevation may indicate ongoing inflammatory/thrombotic milieu that could accompany AKI risk, but evidence is indirect. The mean aggregation further dilutes any acute signal.

In the 25–36h window, MPV may weakly track systemic inflammation or microvascular dysfunction associated with AKI, but it remains nonspecific. As a mean, it is less informative than extremes for acute insults.

An MPV maximum could capture an acute inflammatory/platelet activation spike, but early post-CPB changes are common and not specific for renal injury. Given the 0–12h cap and transient physiology, importance remains low.

MPV peaks in this trajectory phase may reflect ongoing systemic stress that can co-occur with AKI, but the link is indirect and not established as a strong predictor. More kidney-specific hemodynamics/labs would dominate.

Closer to hour 60, an MPV maximum may weakly signal persistent inflammation/microthrombosis that can accompany AKI, but it is still not a direct renal biomarker. Predictive value is likely modest compared with creatinine/urine output/hemodynamics.

Mean platelet volume is not a direct AKI marker; a low minimum MPV in the immediate post-op window is nonspecific and more reflective of perioperative inflammation/transfusion effects than renal injury.
MPV minima remain a weak, nonspecific signal for AKI and are not a primary driver of renal hypoperfusion or nephrotoxicity.
Even close to the outcome window, MPV minimum is not an established predictor of creatinine rise after cardiac surgery compared with hemodynamics, lactate, and renal labs.
Measurement frequency mainly reflects routine CBC ordering post-cardiac surgery rather than clinician concern for impending AKI.
CBC/MPV ordering frequency is largely protocolized in ICU care and is a weak behavioral proxy for AKI risk.
MPV measurement count is not a targeted AKI surveillance test and provides minimal incremental prognostic information for creatinine_ratio.
Higher average lactate suggests global hypoperfusion/low cardiac output, which can contribute to AKI, but early post-bypass lactate elevations are common and transient (0–12h cap).
Persistently elevated mean lactate in the trajectory phase indicates ongoing hypoperfusion/shock physiology, a recognized contributor to postoperative AKI.
A high lactate peak reflects an acute hypoperfusion insult that can precipitate AKI, but immediate post-op peaks may be influenced by CPB and are less specific (0–12h cap).
A high lactate maximum at 13–24h strongly suggests ongoing or recurrent hypoperfusion/low output state, which is directly linked to subsequent creatinine rise after cardiac surgery.
The minimum lactate is less informative for hypoperfusion burden than the maximum/trajectory and is prone to collinearity with other lactate summaries.
A low lactate minimum does not capture the pathologic insult driving AKI; max (or sustained elevation) is the clinically relevant aggregation.
More frequent lactate checks can reflect clinician concern for shock/low output, but it is a behavioral proxy and early post-op lactate monitoring is often routine.
Increased lactate measurement frequency may indicate ongoing instability prompting surveillance, but it is indirect and should be down-weighted versus physiologic values.
Frequent lactate monitoring late suggests persistent concern for hypoperfusion, but as a utilization feature it remains an indirect proxy rather than a mechanism.
Alkaline phosphatase reflects cholestasis/hepatobiliary processes and is not a typical early driver or marker of AKI; early post-op changes are nonspecific.

Alkaline phosphatase reflects hepatobiliary/bone processes and is not a direct AKI marker; early postoperative elevations may reflect systemic stress or cholestasis rather than renal injury. In the 0–12h epoch, transient derangements are common, so prognostic value for creatinine rise is limited.
Low alkaline phosphatase has no established mechanistic link to postoperative AKI risk. As an early (0–12h) minimum, it is unlikely to capture a renal-relevant insult.

Measurement frequency mainly reflects ordering behavior and routine postoperative lab panels rather than kidney physiology. In 0–12h it is especially likely to be protocol-driven, not AKI-specific suspicion.

Repeat ALP ordering in 13–24h is still more reflective of general hepatic/metabolic monitoring than targeted AKI evaluation. As a behavioral proxy, it provides weak, indirect signal for creatinine trajectory.
Even closer to outcome, ALP measurement frequency is not a typical AKI surveillance test compared with creatinine/urine output. Thus it remains a weak behavioral proxy with limited renal specificity.

Higher RDW is associated with inflammation, anemia, and illness severity, which can correlate with AKI risk, but it is nonspecific. Mean values in 0–12h are also influenced by perioperative transfusion/hemodilution, limiting direct interpretability.

RDW can reflect ongoing systemic stress and has modest associations with adverse outcomes including AKI, but remains indirect. Using the mean reduces sensitivity to acute changes and adds collinearity with other RDW summaries.

Later RDW may track persistent inflammation/transfusion effects and overall severity, indirectly relating to AKI risk. However, the mean is still a smoothed, nonspecific marker and is less pathophysiologically tied to creatinine rise than hemodynamics or renal labs.

An elevated RDW maximum may better capture acute transfusion/hemolysis/inflammatory stress than the mean and can correlate with postoperative complications including AKI. Capped at 3 due to the 0–12h epoch where changes are often transient and perioperative.

A higher RDW maximum in 13–24h may indicate ongoing physiologic stress, bleeding/transfusion, or inflammation, which are associated with AKI risk. As an extreme, it is more informative than the mean but remains indirect.

Persistently high RDW maximum closer to hour 60 can reflect sustained illness severity and transfusion/inflammatory burden, which correlates with AKI risk. It is still not a direct renal biomarker, so importance is moderate.

RDW minimum is not a recognized trigger or marker for AKI and is largely uninformative clinically. In the immediate postoperative window it is especially susceptible to dilutional effects without renal specificity.
A low RDW minimum has no established relationship to renal hypoperfusion or tubular injury. It is unlikely to add meaningful predictive signal beyond other RDW summaries.
RDW minimum remains clinically nonspecific and not mechanistically linked to AKI development. It is unlikely to contribute independent information for creatinine_ratio prediction.

RDW measurement frequency is typically driven by routine CBC ordering after cardiac surgery rather than AKI-specific concern. As a behavioral proxy in 0–12h, it provides minimal renal prognostic value.
CBC/RDW rechecks in 13–24h usually reflect standard monitoring for anemia/bleeding rather than kidney injury surveillance. Therefore it is a weak, indirect indicator for subsequent creatinine rise.
Measurement frequency reflects clinician ordering behavior rather than renal physiology; RDW ordering is not a specific AKI signal. At most it weakly proxies overall acuity/anemia workup.

Hyperchloremia can contribute to renal vasoconstriction and AKI risk, but the early post-bypass period has transient electrolyte shifts and mean values dilute acute peaks. Prefer extremes over mean to capture clinically relevant chloride load.

Sustained chloride elevation may reflect ongoing saline load and metabolic acidosis risk, but mean remains less informative than max/min for AKI-related insults. Collinearity control: cap because max/min better capture pathology.

Closer to outcome, persistent hyperchloremia may matter, but mean still smooths clinically important excursions and is redundant with max/min. Use extremes to represent chloride-related renal perfusion effects.

Peak hyperchloremia can indicate high chloride fluid exposure and risk of hyperchloremic acidosis with renal vasoconstriction, but immediate post-op shifts are common and often transient. Early epoch cap applies.

A high chloride peak in the trajectory phase suggests ongoing chloride-rich resuscitation and acid-base disturbance that can worsen renal perfusion. Still an indirect predictor rather than a direct kidney injury biomarker.

Late peak hyperchloremia is a stronger signal of continued chloride load/acid-base derangement near the AKI window and may correlate with aggressive resuscitation and renal vasoconstriction. Extremes best capture this insult.
Low chloride is less directly linked to AKI than hyperchloremia and may reflect dilution or diuretic effects early after surgery. Early epoch and indirect mechanism limit importance.
Hypochloremia can accompany diuresis or metabolic alkalosis but is not a primary driver of post-cardiac surgery AKI. Provides limited incremental value compared with chloride maxima.
Late low chloride may reflect diuretic therapy or dilutional states, which are not specific for intrinsic kidney injury. Weak/indirect association with creatinine rise.
Frequency of chloride checks mainly reflects routine post-op lab protocols rather than AKI physiology. Early post-op labs are commonly ordered regardless of renal trajectory.
Ordering frequency is a behavioral proxy and chloride is typically monitored routinely in ICU patients. Not a specific indicator that AKI is imminent.
More frequent electrolyte monitoring late may reflect clinician concern for instability/acid-base issues, which can co-occur with AKI. Still an indirect, non-physiologic proxy so kept low.
HDL measurement is not part of AKI evaluation and has no acute physiologic link to post-op creatinine rise. Likely reflects baseline lipid assessment rather than renal risk.
HDL ordering is unrelated to renal perfusion or nephrotoxicity in the ICU setting. Measurement frequency provides no meaningful AKI signal.
Late HDL measurement remains clinically disconnected from AKI mechanisms and is unlikely to be ordered for renal concerns. Provides negligible prognostic value for creatinine_ratio.
Mean neutrophil percentage in the immediate post-op window is a nonspecific inflammation marker and not a direct driver of AKI. Early post-CPB leukocyte shifts are common and often transient.

Persistently elevated neutrophil percentage may reflect ongoing inflammation/infection that can contribute indirectly to AKI risk. As a mean value it is nonspecific and less informative than clear clinical sepsis/hemodynamic variables.
A high peak neutrophil percentage may indicate acute inflammatory stress, but in 0–12h it is frequently surgery/CPB-related and transient. It is an indirect, nonspecific AKI correlate at best.

A higher peak in this trajectory phase can suggest evolving infection/inflammation, which can increase AKI risk indirectly. Still not a direct renal biomarker and prone to collinearity with other inflammatory markers.

Low neutrophil percentage early post-op is not a typical mechanistic predictor of AKI and is often driven by relative lymphocytosis or lab variability. Provides little renal-specific prognostic information.
Minimum neutrophil percentage is not an established AKI predictor and is generally nonspecific. It is unlikely to capture a renal-relevant insult compared with hemodynamics or nephrotoxins.
Measurement frequency mainly reflects routine CBC ordering post-cardiac surgery rather than renal pathophysiology. In 0–12h it is standard-of-care and weakly tied to AKI suspicion.
CBC/neutrophil monitoring frequency is largely a care-pattern variable and not a direct AKI mechanism. It may reflect general acuity but is too nonspecific to be strongly predictive.
More frequent neutrophil checks closer to the outcome can reflect clinician concern for infection/sepsis, which can precipitate AKI. Still a behavioral proxy and should remain low importance.

Lower albumin can reflect hemodilution, capillary leak, and illness severity, which are indirectly associated with AKI risk. In the immediate post-op period it is heavily influenced by fluids/CPB, limiting specificity.
A higher maximum albumin early post-op is not a recognized AKI risk signal and is often driven by baseline status or hemoconcentration. It is less pathologic than low albumin and adds redundancy.
